drills.q: What is a container, mechanically? No product names.
drills.a: An ordinary Linux process created with clone()/unshare() using namespace flags (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time) that limit what it can see, combined with cgroup control-file writes that limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O, process count). No container-specific kernel object exists.

drills.q: Namespaces vs cgroups: what's the actual division of responsibility?
drills.a: Namespaces give visibility isolation (what a process can see: its own PID tree, network stack, mount table). Cgroups give resource isolation (hard limits on CPU, memory, process count, I/O). They are independent kernel subsystems -- a namespaced-only process with no cgroup limits has zero resource ceiling.

drills.q: A container keeps exiting with code 137. Diagnose it.
drills.a: 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL), the OOM killer's signature from exceeding memory.max -- memory is incompressible so there's no throttle equivalent. Check actual memory usage trend against the configured limit rather than assuming an application bug; don't just raise the limit without investigating.

drills.q: Explain why CPU limits throttle but memory limits kill.
drills.a: CPU is compressible -- the kernel just stops scheduling a cgroup's threads for the rest of the cfs_quota_us/cfs_period_us period (default 100ms) and resumes next period. Memory is incompressible -- there's no way to pause already-allocated memory, so crossing memory.max triggers immediate OOM-kill (SIGKILL).

drills.q: Walk through the process chain from docker run to a running container.
drills.a: docker CLI -> dockerd -> containerd (image pull, lifecycle) -> containerd-shim (1 per container, survives containerd restarts, holds stdio) -> runc (OCI runtime: clone()/unshare() + cgroup writes, execs into the container process, then exits) -> kernel. The shim, not runc, remains the container's real parent.

drills.q: What is the security significance of the user namespace specifically?
drills.a: It maps UID 0 inside the container to an unprivileged UID on the host, so even a namespace escape doesn't automatically grant host root. Per runc's own guidance, not mapping host root into the container blocks the most severe class of container escape.

drills.q: Explain OverlayFS's layer model and a real performance surprise it causes.
drills.a: Lowerdir (read-only image layers) + upperdir (per-container writable layer) + workdir. Reads search top-down; writes go to upperdir. Modifying a file that only exists in a lower layer triggers a full copy-up of the entire file into upperdir first, making the first write to a large file measurably slower.

drills.q: Why is a container escape considered more severe than a typical VM escape?
drills.a: Containers share the host kernel with no hypervisor boundary, so an escape lands directly in host kernel context. CVE-2024-21626 (runc fd leak giving host filesystem access) is a concrete example. A VM escape must additionally defeat hardware-enforced hypervisor isolation, a structurally harder bug class.

drills.q: What does pids.max protect against and why is it easy to forget?
drills.a: It caps process/thread count per cgroup, defending against a fork bomb in one container exhausting the host's entire PID table (a host-wide outage, not just that container). It's easy to forget because CPU and memory limits dominate attention while process-count exhaustion is a less common but equally severe host-wide failure mode.

drills.q: cgroups v1 vs v2 -- what changed, and is this settled?
drills.a: v1 used separate per-controller hierarchies with unreliable buffered-I/O accounting. v2 (kernel 4.5, 2016) unifies everything into one hierarchy with more consistent accounting. Most distros default to v2 now, but meaningful production infra (older k8s clusters, some monitoring assuming v1) still runs v1 -- this is a live operational question, not settled history.

drills.q: Design question: a CI system runs arbitrary untrusted pipeline code from external contributors. Would you use plain Docker containers?
drills.a: No, not alone -- shared-kernel isolation means a container-escape CVE compromises the CI host directly, exposing every other tenant. Add a stronger boundary (gVisor's syscall interception, or Kata's per-job lightweight VM) accepting extra overhead as the cost of real isolation for untrusted code; if cost/latency rules that out, at minimum harden with seccomp, no host-root mapping via user namespaces, read-only rootfs, dropped capabilities, and fast patching.
